title: Diffraction of light — single slit diffraction
topicTitle: Diffraction of light — single slit diffraction
notes: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave at an edge or through a narrow opening. It is obvious when the opening is comparable with the wavelength, and easy to miss when the opening is huge.
A single slit of width a has a bright central band. The first dark band on either side is at sinθ = λ / a. A smaller width means a larger angle, so squeezing the slit spreads the light more.

The central band is about twice as wide as each side band, and it holds most of the light. These bands are not the equal Young's fringes. One slit does not have two coherent sources a distance d apart.
Covering half the slit changes the pattern because the width a has changed. It does not simply make the old pattern dimmer with the same angles.
A diffraction grating has many slits. The strong maxima satisfy d sinθ = m λ, where d is the spacing of the slits. The maxima are sharp and are used to measure wavelength.
The single-slit envelope still sits on top of the grating pattern. Orders that fall at a single-slit minimum are missing. That is why a grating spectrum can have a gap.

summary: A single slit spreads light into a wide bright centre, with the first dark fringe at sinθ = λ/a. A narrower slit spreads the light more. A grating produces sharp maxima at d sinθ = m λ, and a single-slit minimum can wipe out a grating order.
